teaching_gems.gem: A two-entry dictionary translates Newtonian fluid statements into relativistic ones: comoving d/dt becomes D/dtau and partial_t + v.grad becomes nabla_u; div v = (1/V) dV/dt becomes div u = (1/V) dV/dtau.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The relativistic section becomes a translation exercise from something the learner already trusts, and each relativistic law has an obvious Newtonian parent.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two-column 'Rosetta stone' card that animates each Newtonian term morphing into its relativistic counterpart, with hover links to the flow sandbox and the spacetime worldline view.

teaching_gems.gem: Give div v a body: follow a tagged parcel of fixed mass and read the divergence as the rate its volume swells.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces an abstract operator with a visible deformation and sets up baryon conservation d(nV)/dtau = 0 directly.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Advect a dyed polygon in a 2D field; show its area growth rate next to the averaged divergence inside it; switch to compressible and incompressible presets.

teaching_gems.gem: The conservation law for T 'says too much'; projecting it along u gives energy conservation and projecting it perpendicular to u gives the equation of motion.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns an opaque tensor identity into two physically named equations and teaches projection as a general GR technique (reused for 3+1 splits).
teaching_gems.app_idea: 1+1 or 2+1 spacetime diagram with a draggable 4-vector (the divergence of T) and the local u; the vector splits live into its u-parallel (energy) and rest-space (momentum) pieces.

teaching_gems.gem: Read the relativistic Euler equation against the geodesic equation: pressure gradients across the flow are the only thing pushing fluid off free fall, so dust is geodesic.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects fluids to the central GR idea of geodesic motion and explains at once why cosmology uses dust and why stars need pressure.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Cloud of fluid elements falling toward a mass with a pressure slider and a gradient-profile editor; geodesic ghosts vs actual flow lines, with the acceleration arrow equal to -P.grad p/(rho + p).

teaching_gems.gem: Dot Euler (in vorticity form) with v to kill the vorticity term and reveal Bernoulli as energy per unit mass conserved along streamlines.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows a familiar formula emerging from a single projection, and makes clear why it holds per streamline rather than everywhere.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Venturi-tube simulation with a bar chart of v^2/2, Phi and h following a chosen streamline; toggle a swirl to show streamlines carrying different constants.

teaching_gems.gem: Bookkeep energy for a fixed set of N baryons (V = N/n) to derive the relativistic first law and see that it matches the projected conservation law.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Links geometry (projection of div T) to thermodynamics (first law) and explains why rho + p, the enthalpy density, appears.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Piston with selectable equations of state; plot rho against n and overlay the slope (rho + p)/n predicted by the energy equation.

teaching_gems.gem: Use u.u = -1 as a term-killer, justified by the familiar v.dv = (1/2) d(v^2).
teaching_gems.why_effective: A one-line trick that removes much index clutter and makes the 4-acceleration's orthogonality to u memorable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Worldline curvature explorer showing u and a = nabla_u u as Lorentz-orthogonal arrows, with a numeric u.a readout pinned at zero.

teaching_gems.gem: Warn early that streamlines are velocity snapshots, not particle paths, unless the flow is steady.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Prevents a stubborn misconception before it forms and prepares the relativistic view of flow lines as worldlines.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Unsteady flow animation with streamlines, pathlines and streaklines drawn in three colours that coincide only when 'steady' is toggled on.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 39.5 asserts partial_t s = 0 in the static frame for any perfect fluid, and concludes (v.grad)s = 0. A perfect fluid only guarantees ds/dt = 0 along the flow; partial_t s = 0 needs steady flow or uniform entropy.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think entropy is frozen at every point in space, and misapply (v.grad)s = 0 to unsteady flows.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State ds/dt = partial_t s + v.grad s = 0 as the perfect-fluid condition and add the steady-flow or homentropic assumption explicitly when dropping either term.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Symbol clash: u denotes specific internal energy (rho = rho0(1 + u)) and the 4-velocity on the same pages of 39.4; phi is both velocity potential and scalar field; omega is vorticity and a volume form.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Index expressions like (rho + p) u^mu u^nu next to rho0(1 + u) invite algebra mistakes and confusion.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: In the course use epsilon or e for specific internal energy, keep u for 4-velocity, and use distinct symbols for velocity potential and inflaton.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The margin equation-of-state list prints the scalar-field case as p = [(phidot/2 + V)/(phidot/2 - V)] rho, with no square and swapped signs. The correct form is p = [(phidot^2/2 - V)/(phidot^2/2 + V)] rho.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sign errors would give the wrong inflation limit (the printed version does not give p close to -rho when the potential dominates).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected formula and check limits: kinetic domination gives p = rho, potential domination gives p = -rho.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Minor printing slips in 39.4: rest-frame T^{ij} = p delta^{ik} (should be delta^{ij}); margin eqn 39.61 uses dt where dtau is meant; the first line of 39.64 carries a stray 0; the relativistic volume rule is called the 'derivative rule' in the margin summary and in the main text although it is the divergence rule; eqn 39.7 writes v^j as a partial derivative. The text export also garbles u^t as u^i in 39.51 and T^{0 mu} in exercise 39.2 (printed correctly).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful readers stall on the inconsistencies; rule names get mixed up.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present cleaned equations and keep the labels 'derivative rule' and 'divergence rule' fixed.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 39.9(d) prints the linearized equation of motion as '0 = [...] delta v + (adot/a) delta v = -grad delta Phi', chaining a zero with a nonzero right side.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The equation as printed is self-contradictory unless grad delta Phi = 0.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Read it as [partial_t + v.grad] delta v + (adot/a) delta v = -grad delta Phi.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 39.8's non-relativistic derivation is internally inconsistent. Replacing (rho + p) by rho while keeping p eta^{mu nu} makes T^{tt} = rho - p instead of approximately rho, and that stray -p is exactly what produces the partial_t p on the left of eqn 39.44. The book then reads that term as an energy source via partial_t p = rho0 partial_t h, which the approximations do not justify. The authors themselves call the argument untidy (margin note 12).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may not see which terms are genuinely leading order and may misidentify the time component as full energy conservation rather than, at leading order, mass conservation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Keep (rho + p) until the end: with u^mu = gamma(1, v) the time component gives partial_t[gamma^2(rho + p) - p] + div[gamma^2(rho + p) v] = 0, whose leading order is mass continuity and whose next order is the Newtonian energy equation. Alternatively go straight to the projection method of 39.4.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The relativistic divergence rule div u = (1/V) dV/dtau is proposed by analogy and extended by covariance rather than derived.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may treat it as a guess and distrust later steps (baryon conservation, energy equation) that depend on it.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Derive it from the Lie derivative of the volume form (L_u of the spatial volume element equals (div u) times it), or in local rest-frame coordinates from the Jacobian of the flow.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The physical meaning of rho + p as inertial mass density (enthalpy density) is never spelled out, though it appears in the energy equation, relativistic Euler, and exercises 39.3 and 39.5.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The key relativistic novelty, that pressure has inertia and gravitates, stays hidden behind algebra.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pause after (39.80) to interpret rho + p, compare with a box of hot gas being harder to accelerate, and connect to the (rho + p) term in the TOV equation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The entropy law d(nsV)/dtau >= 0 is motivated by 'no heat flow between flow lines', which actually implies equality for reversible flow; the inequality is the general second law including dissipation that the chapter otherwise excludes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion about whether perfect fluids can generate entropy.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State: in general entropy per baryon cannot decrease (second law); for a perfect fluid (no viscosity or heat conduction) it is exactly conserved.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The free energy a(n, T) in Example 39.15 is introduced without definition.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers cannot verify p = n^2 (partial a/partial n)_T.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define a = rho/n - Ts (free energy per baryon); then da = (p/n^2) dn - s dT follows from the relativistic first law.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Viscosity and heat flux are dropped entirely; there is no mention of imperfect-fluid terms in T or where they matter (neutron-star mergers, early-universe damping).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may assume every relativistic fluid is perfect.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short sidebar showing the structure of the viscous and heat-flux corrections to T and when they matter.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Bernoulli for irrotational unsteady flow is said to hold with a spatially constant right side, but the constant can depend on time.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor, but can confuse when comparing states at different times.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write the right side as C(t) and note it can be absorbed into phi.

tutor_notes: Check first whether the learner wants the Newtonian fluid or only the relativistic payoff; the book marks this chapter as optional, and a GR-focused learner can start from the relativistic Euler equation, borrowing the Newtonian ideas only as needed.

Opening question: 'If you watch a river from a bridge and from a drifting boat, do you measure the same rate of change of water temperature? Why not?' Use it to introduce the convective derivative before any equations.

Explanation order that works: fields (rho0, v) -> streamlines vs paths -> continuity -> pressure force -> convective derivative -> Euler -> Bernoulli as energy -> div T = 0 contains both -> relativistic dictionary -> four laws by projection -> relativistic Euler vs geodesic.
Check for understanding: ask why a submarine at great depth is not pushed sideways despite enormous pressure (only gradients matter), and why the Bernoulli constant can differ between streamlines.
When reaching 39.4, flag the symbol clash immediately: u is both specific internal energy and 4-velocity. Suggest the learner rewrite rho = rho0(1 + epsilon).
Before the projections, make sure the learner can split an ordinary vector into parts along and perpendicular to a unit vector, then redo it with u.u = -1 to see the sign change in P = g + u x u.
Frame the relativistic Euler equation as 'geodesic equation plus pressure force'; ask: what holds a star up against free fall? What happens to the flow lines of dust?

Common learner question: 'Why rho + p instead of rho?' Answer with inertia of pressure (enthalpy density) and point to exercise 39.5, where the same combination sources gravity in hydrostatic equilibrium.

Common learner question: 'Why does one tensor equation give both energy and momentum laws?' Answer: four component equations; contracting with u picks the time-like one for the comoving observer, and P picks the three spatial ones.
Correct the book's misprints proactively when quoting: scalar-field w = (phidot^2/2 - V)/(phidot^2/2 + V); rest-frame T^{ij} = p delta^{ij}; div u = -(1/rho0) drho0/dtau.
For advanced learners, connect to Part V: the comoving derivative is the Lie derivative along the flow, and continuity is conservation of the mass 3-form (exercise 39.6).
Useful quick numbers: about 1 atm per 10 m of water; radiation sound speed c/sqrt(3); matter-era density contrasts grow in proportion to the scale factor.

Retrieval hook for voice tutoring: dust <-> geodesics; pressure gradient <-> non-geodesic flow; projection along u <-> energy; projection across u <-> momentum; d(nV)/dtau = 0 <-> baryon conservation.
